title: Pointe du Hoc — D-Day, 6 June 1944. The 2nd Ranger Battalion scales a 100-foot cliff to silence Hitler's guns.
body: 6 June 1944. D-Day. Pointe du Hoc, on the Normandy coast between Utah Beach and Omaha. German artillery sit on top of a 100-foot vertical cliff, ranged onto both landing beaches. If those guns fire, the invasion bleeds out before it gets off the sand. Lieutenant Colonel James Earl Rudder is given the job. His unit: the 2nd Ranger Battalion — 225 men. The plan is unprecedented. They will land at the base of the cliff, fire grappling-hook ropes from rocket launchers up the rock face, and climb. While being shot at. While the Germans cut their ropes. The landing craft drift off course in the dark and arrive 40 minutes late, soaked and under fire. The ropes are heavy with seawater and many fall short. They climb anyway — some on bare hands, some on extension ladders borrowed from the London Fire Brigade. Forty-five minutes later, Rangers are on top of the cliff. They overrun the gun positions and discover the casemates are empty — the Germans had moved the guns inland to a hidden orchard. A two-man Ranger patrol finds them, unmanned, and destroys them with thermite grenades. By the time relief arrives two days later, only 90 of the 225 Rangers are still able to fight. Rudder is wounded twice and refuses evacuation. The guns of Pointe du Hoc never fire on the beaches.

metadata.objective: Silence German 155mm coastal artillery overlooking Utah and Omaha beaches
